title: Repeated Substring Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every divisor length versus the KMP prefix-suffix array versus the double concatenation trick.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a string s, determine whether it can be constructed by taking some substring of it and repeating that substring multiple times, one after another, with nothing left over.

blocks.text: Given a string s, determine whether it can be constructed by taking some substring of it and repeating that substring multiple times, one after another, with nothing left over.

blocks.title: Analogy: Wallpaper Made From One Repeating Tile
blocks.text: Like looking at a strip of wallpaper and asking whether the whole strip is just one small tile pattern printed over and over, with no partial tile or leftover section anywhere.

blocks.caption: Check whether the whole string is just one smaller piece, repeated end to end

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["\"ab\" repeated exactly twice reconstructs \"abab\"","a valid repeating unit exists","the unit \"ab\" is strictly shorter than s and repeats with nothing left over"],["Answer","true","a genuine repeating unit was found"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["No substring shorter than the whole string, repeated evenly, reconstructs \"aba\"","no valid repeating unit exists","the only divisor length of 3 shorter than the string itself is 1, and \"a\" repeated 3 times gives \"aaa\", not \"aba\""],["Answer","false","no repeating unit reconstructs the original string"]]}

blocks.text: The substring "abc" repeated exactly 4 times reconstructs the whole string exactly, so the answer is true.
It helps to ask what a genuine repeating structure actually implies about how the string relates to a shifted copy of itself.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The brute force tries every divisor length of n as a candidate unit and rebuilds a full string to compare, treating every candidate length as a completely independent guess with no shared structure.

Observation 2: Find the Index of the First Occurrence already showed that comparing strings can be sped up by summarizing structure instead of comparing characters directly; here the useful structure is how much a prefix of the string already overlaps with a suffix of itself, exactly the "longest proper prefix that is also a suffix" array from the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm.

Observation 3: If s truly has a repeating unit, that self overlap value at the very last position reveals the unit's length directly: n minus that value, and checking whether that length evenly divides n confirms it, without ever trying every divisor separately.

Observation 4: An even simpler reformulation exists: a string with a genuine repeating unit is exactly a string that reappears, shifted, inside itself, so concatenating s with itself and trimming exactly one character off each end turns the question into "does s still appear inside this trimmed double string", reusing the exact substring search idea already introduced in Find the Index of the First Occurrence, confirmed by tracing s equal to "abab" through to true.
Recognizing that a repeating string is one that reappears inside a shifted copy of itself is what replaces trying every divisor length separately with a single, elegant substring search.

Try every possible length that evenly divides the total length of the string as a candidate repeating unit, and check directly whether repeating that candidate the right number of times reconstructs the original string exactly.

items: For every candidate length L that evenly divides the length of s, take the first L characters as a candidate unit.
Repeat that candidate unit length of s divided by L times, and compare the result directly against s.
If any candidate length produces an exact match, return true.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Only lengths up to half of n are tried, since a genuine repeating unit must appear at least twice, so it can never be longer than half the string.
Lengths that do not evenly divide n are skipped immediately, since a repeating unit must fit a whole number of times with nothing left over.
Each surviving candidate length is fully rebuilt and compared directly against s, guaranteeing correctness at the cost of rebuilding a full length string for every candidate.

blocks.text: Every possible divisor length is tried directly, so a true repeating unit, if one exists, is guaranteed to be found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) in the worst case, rebuilding and comparing a full length string for every divisor of n.
Space: O(n), for the repeated candidate string built at each step.
Limitation: each candidate length is checked completely independently, throwing away any structural information about the string itself that could rule out most candidate lengths immediately.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it treats every divisor length as an isolated guess, rebuilding and comparing a whole new string each time instead of learning anything from the string's own structure.

What the prefix-suffix array fixes directly: computing, once, how much every prefix of s overlaps with a suffix ending at the same position captures the string's self similarity in a single linear pass.

What that array reveals at the very last position: if a genuine repeating unit exists, its length is exactly n minus this final overlap value, checkable with one divisibility test instead of trying every divisor.

The core idea: build the prefix-suffix array once, then read off the repeating unit's length directly from its last entry.

Compute the string's own "longest proper prefix that is also a suffix" array, the same preprocessing step used in the Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching algorithm. If the string truly has a repeating unit, then the length of the string minus the value of this array at the very last position must evenly divide the string's length, and that difference is exactly the repeating unit's length.
Build the prefix-suffix array once, then check whether n minus its final value evenly divides n.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, at the last position","9 (the prefix \"abcabcabc\" matches the suffix \"abcabcabc\")"],["Candidate repeating length: 12 minus 9","3"],["Does 3 evenly divide 12","yes"],["Answer","true, with repeating unit \"abc\""]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: the prefix-suffix array directly reveals the repeating unit's length

blocks.text: This works because when a string truly consists of a repeating unit, its longest prefix that is also a suffix must exactly line up one full copy short of the whole string, meaning the amount left uncovered at the end, n minus that overlap value, is precisely one copy of the repeating unit, and that length only produces a genuine repeat when it evenly divides the total length n.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The candidate length equals n itself (no meaningful self overlap exists)","The check explicitly rejects this case","The whole string is never mistaken for its own valid repeating unit"],["The candidate length is strictly less than n and evenly divides it","The candidate is confirmed as a genuine repeating unit","The string is correctly identified as built from repetition"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), building the prefix-suffix array in a single linear pass.
Space: O(n), for the prefix-suffix array.
10. Further Optimization: The Double Concatenation Trick

An even simpler and more elegant check exists: concatenate the string with itself, then remove its very first and very last character. If the original string truly has a repeating unit, the original string must appear somewhere inside that trimmed concatenation. This works because the trimming removes exactly the two positions that would otherwise trivially match the string against itself, leaving a genuine match only possible if a real repeating structure exists. This needs no manually built array at all, just a string concatenation and a single substring search.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Concatenate s with itself","\"abababab\""],["Remove the first and last character","\"bababa\""],["Search for \"abab\" inside \"bababa\"","found starting at index 1"],["Answer","true"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: search for the original string inside a trimmed self concatenation

items: Concatenating s with itself creates every possible cyclic shift of s side by side, one right after another.
Trimming exactly the first and last character removes the two positions where s would trivially match itself at its own natural starting point, without removing any genuine shifted occurrence.
Searching for s inside that trimmed string succeeds only when some non trivial shift of s equals s itself, which is mathematically exactly the condition for a genuine repeating unit to exist.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), assuming an efficient linear time substring search is used underneath.
Space: O(n), for the doubled and trimmed string.

blocks.text: Both the prefix-suffix array approach and the double concatenation trick reach the same O(n) time complexity, but the concatenation trick is simpler to implement correctly under interview pressure, since it relies only on a well understood string search rather than a manually built array.

items: Only checking divisor lengths up to n divided by 2 without also handling the case where no divisor produces a match at all, meaning the whole string itself is the only "repeating unit" (which never counts as a valid answer, since a true repeat needs at least 2 copies).
Forgetting to trim exactly one character off each end in the double concatenation trick, which would let the original string trivially match itself even when no real repeat exists.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["A single character string","Can never be built from a strictly shorter repeating unit and always returns false."],["A string where the only matching length is the full string itself","Correctly returns false since that is not a genuine repetition."]]}

blocks.text: Offer the double concatenation trick as the cleaner solution to present under time pressure, but be ready to explain the prefix-suffix array approach too, since it reveals a deeper structural reason why the trick actually works.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do better than checking every divisor", think: the KMP prefix-suffix array, or the simpler double concatenation trick.
If the interviewer says "why does trimming the concatenation work", think: trimming removes exactly the trivial self match at the string's own natural position, leaving only genuine shifted matches possible.
If the interviewer says "what is the actual repeating unit, not just whether one exists", think: the prefix-suffix array approach directly reveals the unit's length, n minus the array's last value.

items: Why does trimming exactly one character off each end of the doubled string prevent a trivial false positive?

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space. Optimized (prefix-suffix array): O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized (double concatenation): O(n) time, O(n) space, with simpler implementation.

items: Pattern: the Knuth-Morris-Pratt prefix-suffix array, further reduced to the elegant double concatenation trick.

Core Idea: a string built from a repeating unit is exactly a string that reappears, shifted, inside a copy of itself, whether revealed through the prefix-suffix array's final value or through a direct search inside a trimmed self concatenation.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for both optimized versions.
Space: O(n) for all three approaches.
Most Important Observation: genuine repetition and self overlap under a shift are the same underlying property, viewed through two different but equally valid lenses.
Interview Difficulty: the double concatenation trick is short to write but easy to forget the trimming step for; the prefix-suffix array is more work but reveals the actual repeating unit's length.
One line memory trick: trim one character off each end of s doubled, and check if s still hides inside.
